name: Maykulan
confidence_why: The only description of the Mayi languages, Breen 1981, states initial main stress for Ngawun and says nothing about stress in Mayi-Kulan or Mayi-Yapi, so the initial trochaic pattern that StressTyp2 lists for Maykulan is carried over from a sister language rather than attested for this one.
catalog_citation: Breen, Gavan. 1981. The Mayi Languages of the Queensland Gulf Country. AIAS new series 29. Canberra: Australian Institute of Aboriginal Studies. Chapter 2 'Phonology' (archive.org Rosetta Project scan rosettaproject_nxn_phon-1, printed pp. 21-29).
catalog_locator: §2.3 'Stress and intonation', printed p. 25 (p. 5), read as page scan; §2.5 'Notes on other Mayi communalects', p. 29, read in full (silent on stress).
catalog_quote: 2.3 Stress and intonation. The main stress on a word is almost always on the first syllable. Occasionally there is a secondary stress on the second syllable of a trisyllabic word. In a four-syllable word there may be a secondary stress on the third syllable, especially if the word is a reduplicated form. In a longer word secondary stress tends to fall on the first syllable of a disyllabic bound morpheme, if any (for example [íkalamùndʊ] 'grass-ABL'), or otherwise on odd-numbered non-final syllables (e.g. [wánatʸùŋkaṛi] 'moon'). For purposes of stress the first vowel of suffixes of the form -VC(C)V normally counts as part of the preceding morpheme. Thus [ímbamìrɪŋgi] not [ímbamɪrìŋgi], although the latter seems to be possible. The word /puṛiŋkir/ 'tomorrow' is exceptional in that the main stress frequently falls on the second syllable, the first vowel then being centralised to [ə] and of…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote confirmed verbatim at page-image grade on Breen 1981 p. 25 (held; scanned text concurs). (2) The deciding work is the sole modern description of Mayabic (Breen 1981, AIAS monograph, salvage data); its stress section is about Ngawun (ngaw1240), and §2.5 — the book's own list of inter-communalect differences — never mentions stress. The catalog already handles the identity problem correctly: the rule is keyed to ngaw1240 (separate record) and mayk1239 is 'undetermined' with the StressTyp2/WALS transfer flagged as a contradiction; no merge or reclassify is indicated. (3) No better or newer source exists: Glottolog 5.3 lists only Breen 1981 as grammar-type for either languoid, the rest being 19th-c. wordlists, a general textbook (Blake 1991) and reviews; the languages are extinct, so no instrumental/JIPA work is possible;or

sources.note: Our 'undetermined' coding rests on ch. 2 describing Ngawun and §2.5 being silent on stress; any stress remark in the Mayi-Kulan/Mayi-Yapi grammatical sections (Breen recorded Mayi-Kulan from Cherry O'Keefe himself) would decide whether the initial-stress description transfers to mayk1239 (reading A, as StressTyp2/WALS assume) or not.
